children.title: Order of Operations
children.summary: BEDMAS tells you which operation to do first when an expression has several mixed together. Get the order wrong and you get a completely different (wrong) answer — even though every individual step looks correct.
children.content:
# Order of Operations ## The Idea When an expression has more than one operation in it, you can't just work left to right — you have to follow a fixed order, or two different people could get two different answers from the exact same expression. That order is **BEDMAS**: - **B**rackets — work out anything inside `( )`, `[ ]`, or `{ }` first, innermost brackets first - **E**xponents — evaluate powers like `3²` or `(-4)³` - **D**ivision and **M**ultiplication — done together, left to right, whichever comes first - **A**ddition and **S**ubtraction — done together, left to right, whichever comes first The key trap is thinking "Division before Multiplication" and "Addition before Subtraction" just because of the order the letters appear in the acronym. They're actually **tied pairs** — you do whichever one appears first as you read left to right. For example, `8 ÷ 2 × 4` is **not** `8 ÷ (2 × 4) = 1`. Division comes first as you read it, so it's `(8 ÷ 2) × 4 = 16`. ## Worked Example Evaluate `-4 + 2[3 - (7 - 10)²] ÷ 3`. ``` -4 + 2[3 - (7 - 10)²] ÷ 3 = -4 + 2[3 - (-3)²] ÷ 3 innermost brackets first: 7 - 10 = -3 = -4 + 2[3 - 9] ÷ 3 exponent: (-3)² = 9 = -4 + 2[-6] ÷ 3 finish the bracket: 3 - 9 = -6 = -4 + (-12) ÷ 3 multiplication: 2 × (-6) = -12 = -4 + (-4) division: -12 ÷ 3 = -4 = -8 addition last ``` **Answer: -8** Notice the brackets get resolved from the inside out — the round brackets `( )` around `7 - 10` had to be dealt with before the square brackets `[ ]` around the whole `3 - (...)²` piece could be finished, since the square brackets depended on that result.
Work down the stack: brackets first, exponents next, then multiplication/division and addition/subtraction as tied pairs done left to right.
## Common Mistakes - Doing multiplication before division automatically, instead of whichever comes first left to right (same for addition/subtraction). - Simplifying outer brackets before the ones nested inside them. - Squaring before applying a negative sign that isn't inside the brackets — `-3²` is `-9`, but `(-3)²` is `9`. ## Quick Gut-Check Brackets first (inside out), then exponents, then multiplication and division together left to right, then addition and subtraction together left to right.

children.title: Operations with Integers
children.summary: Adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing negative numbers all follow predictable sign rules. Once you picture integers as positions and moves on a number line, the rules stop feeling arbitrary.
children.content:
# Operations with Integers ## The Idea Think of every integer as a position on a number line, and every operation as a move along it. **Adding and subtracting** are about direction: - Adding a positive number moves you right. - Adding a negative number moves you left. - Subtracting a number is the same as adding its opposite: `a - b = a + (-b)`. So subtracting a negative flips into moving right — `4 - (-3)` is the same move as `4 + 3`. **Multiplying and dividing** follow a sign rule instead of a direction rule: - Same signs (both positive or both negative) → the answer is **positive**. - Different signs (one positive, one negative) → the answer is **negative**. This works for both operations: `(-4) × (-2) = 8`, but `(-4) × 2 = -8`. Same for division: `(-15) ÷ (-3) = 5`, but `15 ÷ (-3) = -5`. ## Worked Example Evaluate `(-15) ÷ 3 + (-4) × (-2) - 7`. ``` (-15) ÷ 3 + (-4) × (-2) - 7 = -5 + (-4) × (-2) - 7 division first (÷ and × before + and -): (-15) ÷ 3 = -5 = -5 + 8 - 7 multiplication: different-then-same? both negative, so (-4)×(-2)=8 = 3 - 7 add left to right: -5 + 8 = 3 = -4 subtract: 3 - 7 = -4 ``` **Answer: -4** It's worth checking the multiplication and division sign rule separately too: evaluate `(-6) × (-3) ÷ (-2)`. Working left to right, `(-6) × (-3) = 18` (same signs, positive), then `18 ÷ (-2) = -9` (different signs, negative). Notice you re-apply the sign rule at every single step — it doesn't "carry over" from one operation to the next.
4 - (-3) lands on 7: subtracting a negative is the same move as adding a positive.
## Common Mistakes - Forgetting to flip a double negative: `6 - (-2)` is `8`, not `4`. - Applying the multiplication/division sign rule to addition — `(-3) + (-5)` is `-8`, not `+8`; that rule only applies to × and ÷. - Losing track of a negative sign when it's the very first term in an expression. ## Quick Gut-Check For + and -, think "moves on a line." For × and ÷, think "same signs give positive, different signs give negative."

children.title: Exponent Rules
children.summary: An exponent tells you how many times to multiply a base by itself, but brackets around a negative base change everything. This lesson covers negative bases, zero and negative exponents, and dividing powers with the same base.
children.content:
# Exponent Rules ## The Idea `aⁿ` means "multiply `a` by itself `n` times." The tricky part in Grade 9 isn't the multiplying — it's watching exactly what the exponent is attached to, especially when negative numbers are involved. **Brackets matter with negative bases.** `(-2)³` means the base is `-2`, so you multiply `(-2) × (-2) × (-2) = -8`. But `-2³` (no brackets) means "the opposite of `2³`" — the exponent only applies to the `2`, so it's `-(2³) = -8` too when the exponent is odd... but watch what happens with an **even** exponent, where the difference actually shows up: ``` (-2)² = (-2) × (-2) = 4 base is -2, squared -2² = -(2 × 2) = -4 exponent applies to 2 only, then negate ``` Same digits, opposite signs — because the brackets decide whether the negative sign is part of the base. **Zero exponent:** any nonzero number raised to the power `0` equals `1`. For example, `5⁰ = 1`. You can see why by looking at the quotient rule below: `5³ ÷ 5³ = 5^(3-3) = 5⁰`, but anything divided by itself is also `1`, so `5⁰` must equal `1`. **Negative exponent:** a negative exponent means "reciprocal," not "negative number." `x⁻ⁿ = 1/xⁿ`. For example, `2⁻³ = 1/2³ = 1/8`. **Dividing powers with the same base:** subtract the exponents, `xᵃ ÷ xᵇ = xᵃ⁻ᵇ`. This still works even when the result is a negative exponent. ## Worked Example Evaluate `3² ÷ 3⁵` and `4⁻²`. ``` 3² ÷ 3⁵ = 3^(2-5) = 3⁻³ = 1/3³ = 1/27 4⁻² = 1/4² = 1/16 ``` **Answers: 1/27 and 1/16**
Same digits, opposite answers: (-2)² includes the negative in the base, -2² does not.
## Common Mistakes - Treating `-2²` and `(-2)²` as the same thing. - Thinking a negative exponent makes the value negative — `2⁻³ = 1/8`, a small positive number, not `-8`. - Forgetting `x⁰ = 1` and instead writing `x⁰ = 0`. - Multiplying the base by the exponent instead of subtracting exponents when dividing same-base powers. ## Quick Gut-Check No brackets around a negative base means the exponent skips the sign. Negative exponent means "flip to a fraction," not "make negative." Same base, dividing → subtract exponents.

children.title: Fractions and Ratios
children.summary: Fractions can only be added or subtracted once they share a denominator, ratios simplify the same way fractions do, and comparing numbers in mixed forms is easiest once everything is converted to decimals.
children.content:
# Fractions and Ratios ## The Idea You can't add or subtract fractions unless the pieces are the same size — that means the same denominator. If the denominators don't match, find a **common denominator** (usually the lowest common multiple of the two denominators), rewrite each fraction as an equivalent fraction with that denominator, then add or subtract the numerators only. A **ratio** compares two quantities and simplifies exactly like a fraction: divide both terms by their greatest common factor. The ratio `18:24` simplifies to `3:4` by dividing both terms by `6`. When you need to **compare** numbers given in different forms — fractions, decimals, percents — convert everything to the same form first (decimals are usually fastest) so you're comparing apples to apples. ## Worked Example: Adding Fractions Evaluate `2/3 + 3/4 - 1/6`. The lowest common denominator for 3, 4, and 6 is 12. ``` 2/3 = 8/12 (×4/4) 3/4 = 9/12 (×3/3) 1/6 = 2/12 (×2/2) 8/12 + 9/12 - 2/12 = 15/12 = 5/4 = 1 1/4 ``` **Answer: 5/4, or 1 1/4** ## Worked Example: Simplifying a Ratio Simplify the ratio `18:24`. ``` GCF of 18 and 24 is 6 18 ÷ 6 = 3 24 ÷ 6 = 4 18:24 = 3:4 ``` **Answer: 3:4** ## Worked Example: Comparing Forms Order `3/5`, `0.55`, and `58%` from least to greatest. ``` 3/5 = 0.6 0.55 = 0.55 58% = 0.58 ``` **Answer: 0.55 < 58% < 3/5**
Rewriting 2/3 and 3/4 over a common denominator of 12 makes the shaded amounts directly comparable.
## Common Mistakes - Adding numerators and denominators straight across (`2/3 + 3/4 ≠ 5/7`) instead of finding a common denominator. - Simplifying a ratio by subtracting instead of dividing both terms by their greatest common factor. - Comparing `0.55` and `58%` by ignoring the percent sign and treating `58` as bigger than `0.55` without converting it to `0.58` first. ## Quick Gut-Check Same denominator before adding or subtracting fractions. Divide both ratio terms by their GCF to simplify. Convert everything to decimals before comparing mixed forms.

children.title: Percent and Estimation
children.summary: Finding a percent of a number is just multiplying by a decimal, and estimating a square root is about locating it between the two nearest perfect squares. Both are skills you'll lean on constantly later in the course.
children.content:
# Percent and Estimation ## The Idea **Percent means "out of 100."** To find a percent of a number, convert the percent to a decimal (divide by 100) and multiply. `35%` becomes `0.35`, so "35% of 220" is `0.35 × 220`. **Estimating a square root** that isn't a perfect square works by bracketing it between two perfect squares you already know. To estimate `√50`, think about which perfect squares are closest: `7² = 49` and `8² = 64`. Since `49 < 50 < 64`, `√50` must be between `7` and `8`. Because `50` is much closer to `49` than to `64`, `√50` is closer to `7` — roughly `7.1`. ## Worked Example: Percent of a Number Find 35% of 220. ``` 35% = 0.35 0.35 × 220 = 77 ``` **Answer: 77** ## Worked Example: Estimating a Square Root Estimate `√50` to one decimal place. ``` 7² = 49 and 8² = 64 49 < 50 < 64, so 7 < √50 < 8 50 is 1 away from 49 but 14 away from 64, so √50 is much closer to 7. Check: 7.1² = 50.41 (very close to 50) √50 ≈ 7.1 ``` **Answer: √50 is between 7 and 8, closer to 7 — about 7.1** This same bracketing technique works for any non-perfect square. To estimate `√85`, note `9² = 81` and `10² = 100`, so `√85` is between 9 and 10 — and since 85 is much closer to 81 than to 100, the estimate should land closer to 9 (about 9.2).
√50 sits between the perfect squares 49 and 64, much closer to 7 than to 8.
## Common Mistakes - Multiplying by the whole percent number instead of its decimal form (using `35` instead of `0.35`). - Assuming a square root that isn't a whole number is "in the middle" of its two bracketing whole numbers, rather than checking which perfect square it's actually closer to. - Mixing up `√50` with `50 ÷ 2` — a square root is not the same as dividing by 2. ## Quick Gut-Check Percent of a number: divide the percent by 100, then multiply. Square root estimate: find the two nearest perfect squares, then judge which one it's closer to.

children.title: Collecting Like Terms
children.summary: Like terms have the exact same variable raised to the exact same exponent, so they can be combined into one term. The sign in front of a term always travels with it, which is where most errors happen.
children.content:
# Collecting Like Terms ## The Idea **Like terms** have the same variable(s) raised to the same exponent — `3x` and `-7x` are like terms, but `3x` and `3x²` are not, because the exponents don't match. Simplifying an expression means grouping like terms together and combining them by adding or subtracting their coefficients. The one habit that prevents almost every mistake here: **the sign in front of a term belongs to that term.** In `5x - 3y`, the term is `-3y`, not `3y` with a separate subtraction floating in front of it. When you rearrange terms to group them, the sign travels along with the term it's attached to. ## Worked Example Simplify `5x - 3y + 2x² - 7x + 4y - x²`. ``` 5x - 3y + 2x² - 7x + 4y - x² Group by matching term: x² terms: 2x² - x² = x² x terms: 5x - 7x = -2x y terms: -3y + 4y = y Combined: x² - 2x + y ``` **Answer: x² - 2x + y** Notice that the order the terms happen to be written in doesn't matter — `2x²` could just as easily have been the last term instead of the third. What matters is that every term keeps the sign that was directly in front of it when you regroup, so `- x²` stays negative wherever it moves.
Terms sort into bins by variable and exponent; each bin's contents combine into one simplified term.
## Common Mistakes - Dropping or forgetting the sign attached to a term when regrouping it. - Combining `2x²` and `-x` as if they were like terms — the exponents differ, so they can't merge. - Adding coefficients but also multiplying the variable part, writing `2x - 7x` as `-5x²` instead of `-5x`. ## Quick Gut-Check Only combine terms with identical variables and identical exponents, and always carry the sign in front of a term along with it.

children.title: Expanding Expressions
children.summary: The distributive property lets you multiply a single term into everything inside a bracket. When that outside term is negative, every term inside the bracket flips sign as it comes out.
children.content:
# Expanding Expressions ## The Idea The **distributive property** says a term multiplied against a bracket gets multiplied into every term inside it: ``` a(b + c) = ab + ac ``` This still works when `a` is negative — it just means every term that comes out of the bracket changes sign. `-3(x - 5)` distributes as `-3 × x` and `-3 × (-5)`, giving `-3x + 15`. The double negative inside is easy to lose track of, so it helps to expand one term at a time rather than rushing. Compare the two: `4(2x + 1) = 8x + 4` (positive out front, signs inside stay the same), but `-4(2x + 1) = -8x - 4` (negative out front, both signs flip). The bracket's contents don't change — only the sign attached to each term when it leaves the bracket changes, and it changes according to the usual multiplication sign rule. ## Worked Example Expand and simplify `2(3x - 4) - 5(x - 2)`. ``` 2(3x - 4) - 5(x - 2) = 2(3x) + 2(-4) - 5(x) - 5(-2) distribute both brackets = 6x - 8 - 5x + 10 -5 × (-2) = +10 = (6x - 5x) + (-8 + 10) collect like terms = x + 2 ``` **Answer: x + 2**
Distributing -5 flips the sign of every term inside the bracket: -5 × x stays negative, -5 × (-2) becomes positive.
## Common Mistakes - Distributing into only the first term inside the bracket and forgetting the second. - Multiplying a negative outside term by a negative inside term and getting the sign wrong — two negatives give a positive. - Forgetting to distribute the negative sign at all when the term out front is `-a` rather than `-1 × a` written explicitly. ## Quick Gut-Check Multiply the outside term into every term inside the bracket, and let the sign rules for multiplication decide the sign of each result.

children.title: Evaluating Expressions
children.summary: Evaluating an expression means replacing each variable with a given number and simplifying using order of operations. Wrapping negative substitutions in brackets is the single habit that prevents the most sign errors.
children.content:
# Evaluating Expressions ## The Idea To evaluate an algebraic expression, replace every variable with the value you're given, then simplify using BEDMAS — brackets, exponents, multiplication/division, addition/subtraction, in that order. The most important habit: **put substituted negative values in brackets.** If `x = -3` and the expression has `x²`, write `(-3)²`, not `-3²`. Those two are different numbers — `(-3)² = 9` while `-3²` (without brackets around the substituted value) would incorrectly suggest `-9`. Using brackets when you substitute keeps the negative sign attached to the value it belongs to. ## Worked Example Evaluate `2x² - 3x + 5` when `x = -3`. ``` 2x² - 3x + 5 = 2(-3)² - 3(-3) + 5 substitute x = -3, using brackets = 2(9) - 3(-3) + 5 exponent first: (-3)² = 9 = 18 - (-9) + 5 multiply: 2(9)=18 and -3(-3)=9, so this term is -(-9) = 18 + 9 + 5 = 32 ``` **Answer: 32** The same substitution habit applies with more than one variable. To evaluate `a² - 2ab` when `a = -2` and `b = 3`, substitute both with brackets around the negative value: `(-2)² - 2(-2)(3) = 4 - (-12) = 4 + 12 = 16`. Every variable gets replaced at once, then the whole thing simplifies with BEDMAS as usual.
Every x in the expression is replaced by (-3) in brackets, so the exponent and multiplication apply to the whole value including its sign.
## Common Mistakes - Substituting a negative value without brackets, then applying an exponent to only the digit and not the sign. - Skipping order of operations after substituting — multiplying before an exponent has been applied. - Substituting into only one occurrence of the variable when it appears more than once in the expression. ## Quick Gut-Check Replace every variable with its value in brackets, then simplify with BEDMAS exactly as if the bracketed value were any other number.

children.title: Solving Two-Step Equations
children.summary: A two-step equation needs two inverse operations to isolate the variable, applied in the reverse of the order they were built in. Undo addition or subtraction first, then undo multiplication or division.
children.content:
# Solving Two-Step Equations ## The Idea An equation like `2x + 7 = 19` was built in a specific order: start with `x`, multiply by `2`, then add `7`. To solve it, you undo those steps in **reverse order** — undo the addition first, then undo the multiplication. Whatever you do to one side of the equation, you must do to the other side too, to keep it balanced. The same logic applies when the variable term involves division, like `x/4 - 3 = 2`: undo the subtraction first (add 3 to both sides), then undo the division (multiply both sides by 4). ## Worked Example Solve `2x + 7 = 19`. ``` 2x + 7 = 19 2x + 7 - 7 = 19 - 7 subtract 7 from both sides (undo the +7) 2x = 12 2x ÷ 2 = 12 ÷ 2 divide both sides by 2 (undo the ×2) x = 6 ``` Check: `2(6) + 7 = 12 + 7 = 19` ✓ **Answer: x = 6** Now one with division in the variable term: solve `x/4 - 3 = 2`. ``` x/4 - 3 = 2 x/4 = 5 add 3 to both sides x = 20 multiply both sides by 4 ``` Check: `20/4 - 3 = 5 - 3 = 2` ✓ **Answer: x = 20**
The equation was built as ×2 then +7; solving undoes those steps in reverse — subtract 7 first, then divide by 2.
## Common Mistakes - Undoing the operations in the same order they were applied instead of reverse order (dividing before subtracting). - Performing an operation on only one side of the equation instead of both. - Forgetting to multiply back through when the variable term is a fraction like `x/4`. ## Quick Gut-Check Undo addition or subtraction first, then undo multiplication or division — the reverse of how the expression was built — and always apply each step to both sides.

children.title: Solving Multi-Step Equations
children.summary: When an equation has a bracket to expand or the variable on both sides, clear those complications first, then solve it the same way as any two-step equation. The strategy is always: simplify, collect, isolate.
children.content:
# Solving Multi-Step Equations ## The Idea Some equations aren't ready to solve right away — there's a bracket to expand first, or the variable shows up on both sides. The strategy is always the same three moves: 1. **Simplify** each side separately — expand any brackets, collect like terms. 2. **Collect** the variable terms onto one side and the constants onto the other. When a term crosses the equals sign, it changes sign (this is really just subtracting or adding it to both sides at once). 3. **Isolate** the variable using inverse operations, same as a two-step equation. ## Worked Example: Expanding First Solve `3(x + 2) = 2x + 13`. ``` 3(x + 2) = 2x + 13 3x + 6 = 2x + 13 expand the bracket 3x + 6 - 2x = 2x + 13 - 2x subtract 2x from both sides x + 6 = 13 x + 6 - 6 = 13 - 6 subtract 6 from both sides x = 7 ``` Check: `3(7 + 2) = 3(9) = 27`, and `2(7) + 13 = 14 + 13 = 27` ✓ **Answer: x = 7** ## Worked Example: Variable on Both Sides Solve `5x - 4 = 2x + 11`. ``` 5x - 4 = 2x + 11 5x - 4 - 2x = 11 move 2x to the left (subtract 2x from both sides) 3x - 4 = 11 3x = 15 add 4 to both sides x = 5 divide both sides by 3 ``` **Answer: x = 5**
Moving 2x from the right side to the left flips its sign — the same result as subtracting 2x from both sides.
## Common Mistakes - Distributing into only part of a bracket before collecting like terms. - Moving a term across the equals sign without flipping its sign. - Collecting variable terms on one side but forgetting to also move the constant terms fully to the other side before dividing. ## Quick Gut-Check Expand brackets and simplify both sides first, then gather all variable terms on one side and constants on the other, flipping signs as terms cross the equals sign, and finish by isolating the variable.

children.title: Slope and Rate of Change
children.summary: Slope measures how steep a line is and which way it tilts — it's a rate of change, `rise/run`. Learn to find it from two points, from a graph, or straight off an equation `y = mx + b`.
children.content:
# Slope and Rate of Change ## The Idea Slope tells you how steep a line is and which way it's tilted. More precisely, slope is a **rate of change**: it measures how much `y` changes for every one unit that `x` increases. If you've ever described a hill as "rising 2 metres for every 10 metres you walk," you've already used the idea of slope — it's just rise over run. Slope shows up anywhere a quantity changes at a steady rate: distance over time, cost per hour, or how a value on a graph climbs or drops as you move along the x-axis. ## Three Ways to Find Slope **1. From two points.** If you know two points `(x₁, y₁)` and `(x₂, y₂)` on a line, the slope is: ``` m = (y₂ - y₁) / (x₂ - x₁) ``` This is "rise" (change in y) divided by "run" (change in x). **2. From a graph.** Pick two points where the line crosses clear grid intersections, then count the vertical distance (rise) and horizontal distance (run) between them. **3. From an equation.** If the equation is written in slope-intercept form, `y = mx + b`, the slope is simply the coefficient `m` — the number multiplied by `x`. ## Positive, Negative, Zero, and Undefined Slope - **Positive slope**: the line rises as you move left to right. - **Negative slope**: the line falls as you move left to right. - **Zero slope**: the line is perfectly horizontal — `y` never changes. - **Undefined slope**: the line is perfectly vertical — `x` never changes, so you'd be dividing by zero. ## Worked Example Find the slope of the line through `(1, 3)` and `(4, 9)`. ``` m = (y₂ - y₁) / (x₂ - x₁) m = (9 - 3) / (4 - 1) m = 6 / 3 m = 2 ``` The slope is 2: for every 1 unit `x` increases, `y` increases by 2.
Slope is the ratio of rise (vertical change) to run (horizontal change) between any two points on the line.
## Common Mistakes - Subtracting in mismatched order — if you compute `y₂ - y₁` on top, you must use the same two points in the same order for `x₂ - x₁` on the bottom. - Mixing up zero slope and undefined slope: horizontal lines have slope 0 (a well-defined, flat rate); vertical lines have no slope at all — the formula would require dividing by zero. - Forgetting that slope is a ratio — `6/3` and `2/1` describe the exact same slope, just before and after simplifying. ## Quick Gut-Check Steep and climbing → large positive slope. Flat → slope of 0. Falling → negative slope. Straight up and down → undefined.

children.title: Equations of Lines
children.summary: Every line can be written as `y = mx + b`, where `m` is the slope and `b` is the y-intercept. Learn to build that equation from given information, and to read `m` and `b` off an equation — even one that needs rearranging first.
children.content:
# Equations of Lines ## The Idea Every straight, non-vertical line can be written in **slope-intercept form**: ``` y = mx + b ``` `m` is the slope (how steep the line is, and which way it tilts), and `b` is the **y-intercept** — the value of `y` when `x = 0`, which is exactly where the line crosses the y-axis. Once you know these two numbers, you know the entire line. ## Writing an Equation from Slope and Y-Intercept If you're told the slope and y-intercept directly, just plug them into the form. Example: slope `-2`, y-intercept `5`: ``` y = -2x + 5 ``` No solving required — the numbers slot straight in. ## Reading m and b Off an Equation If an equation is already written as `y = mx + b`, read the slope and y-intercept straight off. But equations aren't always given in this tidy form — sometimes you need to rearrange first. Example: `2x + 3y = 6`. Solve for `y`: ``` 2x + 3y = 6 3y = -2x + 6 y = (-2/3)x + 2 ``` Now the slope is `-2/3` and the y-intercept is `2`. ## Worked Example A line has slope `3` and y-intercept `-4`. Write its equation, then find `y` when `x = 5`. ``` y = 3x - 4 y = 3(5) - 4 y = 15 - 4 y = 11 ``` The equation is `y = 3x - 4`, and the point `(5, 11)` lies on the line.
b is where the line crosses the y-axis; m is the rise-over-run slope of the climb from there.
## Common Mistakes - Losing a negative sign on the slope or intercept while rearranging an equation — track signs one term at a time. - Mixing up which axis `b` belongs to — `b` is always the y-intercept, the value of `y` when `x = 0`, not the x-intercept. - Trying to read off `m` and `b` before fully isolating `y` — you can't read the slope directly from `2x + 3y = 6`; you must solve for `y` first. ## Quick Gut-Check `y = mx + b`: `m` is the number attached to `x`, `b` is the lone number added or subtracted at the end — the height where the line crosses the y-axis.

children.title: Intercepts
children.summary: The x-intercept and y-intercept are where a line crosses each axis. Find them by setting the *other* variable to zero, and learn what each intercept can mean in a real graph.
children.content:
# Intercepts ## The Idea An **intercept** is a point where a line crosses one of the axes. Every non-horizontal, non-vertical line has exactly one x-intercept and one y-intercept (unless it passes through the origin, where the two are the same point). - The **y-intercept** is where the line crosses the y-axis. At that point, `x = 0`. - The **x-intercept** is where the line crosses the x-axis. At that point, `y = 0`. ## How to Find Them To find the **y-intercept**, substitute `x = 0` into the equation and solve for `y`. To find the **x-intercept**, substitute `y = 0` into the equation and solve for `x`. ## What They Represent In a real-world graph, intercepts often carry meaning. If a graph shows the amount of water in a tank over time, the y-intercept is the starting amount (at time zero), and the x-intercept — if the water is draining — is the moment the tank becomes empty. ## Reading Intercepts Off a Graph If you already have a graph instead of an equation, you don't need to solve anything — just look at where the line physically crosses each axis and read the coordinates directly. This is often the fastest way to find intercepts, but it's only as precise as the graph is drawn, so when exact values matter, solving algebraically from the equation is more reliable. ## Worked Example Find both intercepts of `3x + 2y = 12`. **y-intercept** (set `x = 0`): ``` 3(0) + 2y = 12 2y = 12 y = 6 ``` y-intercept: `(0, 6)` **x-intercept** (set `y = 0`): ``` 3x + 2(0) = 12 3x = 12 x = 4 ``` x-intercept: `(4, 0)`
The y-intercept is where x = 0; the x-intercept is where y = 0.
## Common Mistakes - Setting the wrong variable to zero — to find the x-intercept you set `y = 0` (not `x`), because you want the point ON the x-axis, where the height is zero. - Reporting a single number instead of the full coordinate pair — the x-intercept is the point `(4, 0)`, not just "4," even though naming the value alone is common shorthand once the point is understood. - Assuming every line has both intercepts — a horizontal line like `y = 5` never crosses the x-axis, and a vertical line like `x = 3` never crosses the y-axis. ## Quick Gut-Check Want the y-intercept? Plug in `x = 0`. Want the x-intercept? Plug in `y = 0`. You're always finding where the *other* coordinate is zero.

children.title: Verifying Points on a Line
children.summary: A point lies on a line only if its coordinates make the equation true. Substitute the x-value in, simplify, and compare to the given y-value — a match means the point is on the line.
children.content:
# Verifying Points on a Line ## The Idea A point "lies on" a line if its coordinates make the line's equation true. Checking this is simple: substitute the point's `x`-value into the equation and see what `y`-value comes out. If it matches the point's actual `y`-value, the point is on the line. If it doesn't, the point is off the line. This works because a linear equation is a rule that every point on the line must obey — and no point off the line can satisfy it. ## The Method Given a point `(a, b)` and an equation: 1. Substitute `x = a` into the right side of the equation. 2. Simplify. 3. Compare the result to `b`. If they match, the point is on the line. ## Worked Example Is the point `(2, 5)` on the line `y = 3x - 1`? ``` y = 3x - 1 y = 3(2) - 1 y = 6 - 1 y = 5 ``` The equation gives `y = 5` when `x = 2`, which matches the point's y-coordinate exactly. **Yes, (2, 5) is on the line.** Now check `(2, 8)`: ``` y = 3(2) - 1 = 5 ``` The equation predicts `y = 5`, but the point claims `y = 8`. Since `5 ≠ 8`, **(2, 8) is not on the line.** ## Why This Matters This same substitution check works no matter how the equation is written, not just in `y = mx + b` form. Given `2x + y = 9`, checking whether `(3, 3)` is a solution means substituting both coordinates directly: `2(3) + 3 = 6 + 3 = 9`, which matches, so `(3, 3)` works. The idea is always the same — replace every variable with the coordinate that corresponds to it, then confirm both sides of the equation agree.
(2, 5) sits exactly on the line, so it satisfies the equation. (2, 8) does not fall on the line, so it fails the check.
## Common Mistakes - Substituting the y-value in for `x` by mistake — always plug the x-coordinate into the `x` in the equation. - Stopping after simplifying, without comparing the result to the given y-value — the whole point of the check is that final comparison. - Making an arithmetic slip with negative numbers, especially when the equation or the point involves negative coordinates. Double-check the sign of every term. - Assuming a point is on the line just because it's "close." In algebra, close doesn't count — the two sides must be exactly equal. ## Quick Gut-Check Plug the x-coordinate in, simplify, and see if you land exactly on the given y-coordinate. Match means on the line; mismatch means off it.

children.title: Linear Relations in Context
children.summary: Real situations that change at a steady rate — like a call-out fee plus an hourly charge — can be modelled with `y = mx + b`, where `m` is the rate of change and `b` is the fixed starting value.
children.content:
# Linear Relations in Context ## The Idea Many real situations grow or shrink at a steady rate — and anything that changes by the same amount for every equal step can be modelled with a linear equation, `y = mx + b`. In context: - `m` (the slope) is the **rate of change** — how much the total changes per unit (per hour, per item, per kilometre). - `b` (the y-intercept) is the **starting value** — the amount you begin with before the rate kicks in at all, often a fixed fee or an initial amount. Recognizing which number in a word problem is the rate and which is the fixed starting value is the whole skill here. ## Building the Equation Read the problem for two things: a number that stays the same no matter what ("call-out fee," "starting balance," "initial height") — that's `b` — and a number that's multiplied by something changing ("per hour," "for each," "every kilometre") — that's `m`. ## Worked Example A plumber charges a $50 call-out fee, plus $75 for every hour of work. Let `C` be the total cost in dollars and `h` be the number of hours worked. ``` C = 75h + 50 ``` Here, `m = 75` (the rate: $75 per hour) and `b = 50` (the fixed cost, charged even before any work begins). **Find the cost of a 3-hour job:** ``` C = 75(3) + 50 C = 225 + 50 C = 275 ``` The job costs $275. **Find how many hours fit a $350 budget:** ``` 350 = 75h + 50 300 = 75h h = 4 ``` $350 covers exactly 4 hours of work.
The y-intercept is the fixed fee paid at 0 hours; the slope is the hourly rate that gets added on top.
## Common Mistakes - Swapping the slope and the y-intercept — the fixed fee is paid once and doesn't depend on the variable, so it's always `b`, never `m`. - Forgetting units. A rate of change in context always has units attached (dollars per hour, litres per minute) — a "rate" without units isn't a finished answer. - Trusting the model too far outside where it makes sense — `C = 75h + 50` fits a normal job, but it likely doesn't apply for `h = 0` (no such thing as a 0-hour job) or for absurdly large `h`. ## Quick Gut-Check Ask: "What do I pay even if nothing happens?" That's `b`. Ask: "How much does it change for each extra unit?" That's `m`.

children.title: Area of 2-D Shapes
children.summary: Area measures the surface a flat shape covers. Triangle area is half base times height; circle area is pi times the radius squared — and the radius, never the diameter, is what gets squared.
children.content:
# Area of 2-D Shapes ## The Idea Area measures how much surface a flat shape covers, in square units (like cm² or m²). Every shape has its own formula, but two of the most useful ones in this course are for **triangles** and **circles**. ## Area of a Triangle ``` A = (1/2) · b · h ``` where `b` is the length of the base and `h` is the **height** — the perpendicular (straight up-and-down) distance from the base to the opposite vertex. The height is not the same as a slanted side unless that side happens to meet the base at a right angle. ## Area of a Circle ``` A = π · r² ``` where `r` is the radius — the distance from the centre to the edge. If you're given the diameter instead, remember `r = d/2` and halve it first. ## Worked Examples **Triangle:** base = 8 cm, height = 5 cm. ``` A = (1/2)(8)(5) A = (1/2)(40) A = 20 cm² ``` **Circle:** radius = 4 m. Use `π ≈ 3.14`. ``` A = π(4)² A = π(16) A ≈ 3.14 × 16 A ≈ 50.24 m² ``` ## Composite Shapes Some figures are made of a triangle and a circle (or other shapes) joined together, like a semicircular window sitting on top of a triangular gable. To find the total area, calculate each piece separately with its own formula, then add the results together (or subtract, if one shape is a hole cut out of another). Always check whether a curved edge is a full circle or only part of one — a semicircle's area is half of `πr²`, not the full formula.
Triangle area uses the perpendicular height, not a slanted side. Circle area always squares the radius, not the diameter.
## Common Mistakes - Using the diameter instead of the radius in the circle formula — always square the *radius*. Using the diameter by accident gives an answer four times too large. - Forgetting the `1/2` in the triangle formula — this is the single most common triangle-area error. - Using a slanted side as the "height" of a triangle when it isn't perpendicular to the base. The height must form a right angle with the base. - Leaving the answer without square units — area is always reported in units², never plain units. ## Quick Gut-Check Triangle: half of base times height. Circle: pi times radius squared — and always radius, never diameter.

children.title: Perimeter and Circumference
children.summary: Perimeter is the total distance around a shape's outside — just add up the sides. Circumference is the special name for a circle's perimeter, found with `C = πd` or `C = 2πr`.
children.content:
# Perimeter and Circumference ## The Idea Perimeter is the total distance around the outside of a shape — add up the lengths of every side. **Circumference** is just the special name for the perimeter of a circle, and because a circle has no straight sides to add up, it gets its own formula. ## Perimeter of Rectangles and Polygons For any polygon, perimeter is simply the sum of all side lengths: ``` P = sum of all sides ``` For a rectangle with length `l` and width `w`, this simplifies to: ``` P = 2l + 2w ``` since opposite sides are equal. ## Circumference of a Circle ``` C = π · d or equivalently C = 2π · r ``` where `d` is the diameter and `r` is the radius. Use whichever form matches the measurement you're given. ## Worked Examples **Rectangle:** length = 12 cm, width = 7 cm. ``` P = 2(12) + 2(7) P = 24 + 14 P = 38 cm ``` **Circle:** diameter = 10 m. Use `π ≈ 3.14`. ``` C = π(10) C ≈ 3.14 × 10 C ≈ 31.4 m ``` ## Composite Perimeters Not every shape is a simple rectangle or circle — a running track, for instance, might be two straight sides plus two semicircular ends. To find its perimeter, add the straight sides directly and treat the two semicircular ends together as one full circle's circumference (since two halves make a whole). The same "break it into pieces, then combine" approach works for any composite outline, as long as you're careful only to add lengths that are actually on the outer boundary.
Rectangle perimeter adds all four sides; circle circumference is pi times the diameter straight across.
## Common Mistakes - Confusing perimeter with area — perimeter is a length (measured in units like cm), while area is measured in square units. Mixing up the two formulas is the most common mistake in this whole topic. - Using the radius in the `C = πd` formula, or the diameter in the `C = 2πr` formula, without adjusting first. Match the formula to the measurement you actually have. - Forgetting a side when adding up an irregular polygon's perimeter — sketch the shape and mark each side as you add it, so none get missed. ## Quick Gut-Check Perimeter: walk around the outside and add every side. Circle version: circumference = pi times diameter (or `2πr` — same thing, two ways to say it).

children.title: Volume and Surface Area
children.summary: Volume measures the space inside a 3-D shape; surface area measures the total area of its outside faces. Formulas for rectangular prisms, cubes, and cylinders, with a worked example of each.
children.content:
# Volume and Surface Area ## The Idea **Volume** measures how much space a 3-D shape takes up, in cubic units (cm³, m³). **Surface area** measures the total area of every face on the outside of the shape, in square units — imagine unfolding the shape flat and adding up the area of each piece. ## Rectangular Prisms and Cubes For a rectangular prism with length `l`, width `w`, and height `h`: ``` V = l · w · h SA = 2(lw) + 2(lh) + 2(wh) ``` The surface area formula adds up the areas of all six rectangular faces — front/back, left/right, top/bottom — in matching pairs. A cube is just a rectangular prism where every edge has the same length `s`: ``` V = s³ SA = 6s² ``` ## Cylinders For a cylinder with radius `r` and height `h`: ``` V = π · r² · h SA = 2π · r² + 2π · r · h ``` The volume is the circular base area times the height. The surface area is the two circular ends (`2πr²`) plus the curved side, which unrolls into a rectangle with area `2πr · h`. ## Worked Example A rectangular prism has length 6 cm, width 4 cm, and height 3 cm. ``` V = 6 × 4 × 3 = 72 cm³ SA = 2(6×4) + 2(6×3) + 2(4×3) SA = 2(24) + 2(18) + 2(12) SA = 48 + 36 + 24 SA = 108 cm² ```
A rectangular prism has six rectangular faces; volume is length times width times height.
## Common Mistakes - Mixing up volume and surface area formulas — volume uses cubic units, surface area uses square units. If your answer's units don't match what you were solving for, something went wrong. - Forgetting to double each face pair in the prism's surface area formula — there are six faces total, not three. - Using the diameter instead of the radius in cylinder formulas, since both `r²` and `2πr` specifically need the radius. - Leaving out one of the two circular ends when finding a cylinder's surface area — it's easy to remember the curved side and forget the top and bottom circles. ## Quick Gut-Check Volume = space inside (cubic units). Surface area = area of every outside face added up (square units). For prisms, count all six faces; for cylinders, don't forget both circles.

children.title: Angle Relationships
children.summary: A triangle's interior angles always sum to 180°, a quadrilateral's to 360°, and complementary angle pairs sum to 90°. Use these fixed totals to solve for a missing angle.
children.content:
# Angle Relationships ## The Idea Angles inside certain shapes always add up to a fixed total, no matter how the shape is stretched or skewed. Knowing these fixed totals lets you find a missing angle whenever you know all the others. ## Triangle Angle Sum The three interior angles of any triangle always add up to `180°`: ``` ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180° ``` ## Quadrilateral Angle Sum The four interior angles of any quadrilateral (a four-sided shape) always add up to `360°`: ``` ∠A + ∠B + ∠C + ∠D = 360° ``` This makes sense because any quadrilateral can be split into two triangles by drawing one diagonal, and `2 × 180° = 360°`. ## Complementary Angles Two angles are **complementary** if they add up to exactly `90°`. This often shows up where two angles together form a right angle, like the corner of a square. ``` ∠A + ∠B = 90° ``` ## Worked Examples **Triangle:** two angles are `52°` and `71°`. Find the third. ``` 52 + 71 + x = 180 123 + x = 180 x = 57° ``` **Quadrilateral:** three angles are `90°`, `105°`, and `80°`. Find the fourth. ``` 90 + 105 + 80 + x = 360 275 + x = 360 x = 85° ``` **Complementary pair:** one angle is `34°`. Find its complement. ``` 34 + x = 90 x = 56° ```
The three interior angles of a triangle always add to 180°, so the missing angle is 180° minus the two known angles.
## Common Mistakes - Using `180°` for a quadrilateral instead of `360°` — the sum depends on the number of sides, so double check which shape you're working with. - Confusing complementary (`90°`) with supplementary (`180°`) — a handy trick: "c" for complementary comes before "s" for supplementary, and 90 comes before 180. - Forgetting to add all the known angles together before subtracting from the full sum — total the knowns first, then subtract that total from 180° or 360° to isolate the missing angle. ## Quick Gut-Check Triangle → 180°. Quadrilateral → 360°. Two angles fitting into a right angle → complementary, 90°.

children.title: Measures of Central Tendency
children.summary: Mean, median, and mode each describe a data set's "typical" value differently. This lesson shows how to calculate all three from a small data set, and why the median resists being dragged around by an outlier that skews the mean.
children.content:
# Measures of Central Tendency ## The Idea When you have a list of numbers, you often want one number that describes the "typical" value. That's what a **measure of central tendency** does. There are three common ones — mean, median, and mode — and each answers a slightly different question. - **Mean** — the arithmetic average. Add up all the values and divide by how many there are. - **Median** — the middle value once the data is sorted from smallest to largest. If there are two middle values, average them. - **Mode** — the value that occurs most often. A data set can have one mode, more than one mode, or no mode at all. None of these is "the right one" in every situation — part of the skill is picking the measure that best represents the data. ## Worked Example Five people are at a small family gathering. Their ages are: ``` 12, 14, 14, 15, 65 ``` **Mean:** ``` (12 + 14 + 14 + 15 + 65) ÷ 5 = 120 ÷ 5 = 24 ``` **Median:** the data is already sorted — the middle value (3rd of 5) is: ``` 12, 14, [14], 15, 65 → median = 14 ``` **Mode:** 14 appears twice, more than any other value: ``` mode = 14 ``` Notice the mean (24) is quite a bit higher than every age except one person's. That's because 65 pulls the average upward. The median and mode, both 14, better describe the "typical" age at this gathering — most people there are young teens, not 24-year-olds. ## Why It Matters - **Median resists outliers.** Because the median only cares about position (which value is in the middle), one extreme value barely moves it. The mean, on the other hand, is pulled toward every value — including extreme ones. - **Mode works for non-numeric data.** You can't average "favourite colour," but you can find the most common one. Mode is the only measure of the three that makes sense for categorical data like colours, brands, or survey choices. - **Mean uses every value.** When data doesn't have extreme outliers, the mean is often the most informative measure because it factors in every single data point, not just the middle one or the most frequent one.
Four ages cluster near 12–15, but one outlier at 65 drags the mean up to 24 — the median stays at 14, close to where most of the data actually is.
## Common Mistakes - Forgetting to sort the data before finding the median — the "middle value" only works on sorted data. - Having an **even** number of values and forgetting to average the two middle numbers, instead just picking one of them. - Reporting "no mode" as zero — no mode simply means every value appears the same number of times (often once each). ## Quick Gut-Check Mean uses every value and is sensitive to outliers. Median finds the middle and resists outliers. Mode finds the most frequent value and is the only option for non-numeric data.

children.title: Range and Outliers
children.summary: The range of a data set is its maximum minus its minimum, and an outlier is a value that sits unusually far from the rest of the data. This lesson shows how one outlier can dramatically inflate both the range and the mean.
children.content:
# Range and Outliers ## The Idea The **range** of a data set is the simplest measure of spread: it's just the largest value minus the smallest value. ``` range = maximum − minimum ``` It tells you how far apart the extremes of your data are — but by itself it says nothing about what happens in between. An **outlier** is a value that sits unusually far from the rest of the data. Outliers matter because a single one can badly distort both the range and the mean, making a data set look more spread out — or a "typical" value look bigger or smaller — than it really is. ## Worked Example Six students each did as many push-ups as they could in one minute: ``` 12, 15, 14, 16, 13, 40 ``` **Range (with the outlier):** ``` 40 − 12 = 28 ``` Sorted, five of the six values sit close together (12 to 16), and then there's 40 — clearly an **outlier**, maybe a student who trains competitively. **Range without the outlier**, using just 12, 15, 14, 16, 13: ``` 16 − 12 = 4 ``` Removing a single value drops the range from 28 all the way to 4 — a sign that 40 was doing almost all the work. **Effect on the mean:** ``` With the outlier: (12+15+14+16+13+40) ÷ 6 = 110 ÷ 6 ≈ 18.3 Without the outlier: (12+15+14+16+13) ÷ 5 = 70 ÷ 5 = 14 ``` One value shifts the mean from 14 up to about 18.3 — over four push-ups higher than every single one of the other five students actually did. ## Spotting an Outlier There's no single rule that works perfectly every time, but a good starting check is: does this value sit far outside the cluster where the rest of the data lives? If most values are packed into a narrow range and one value sits noticeably beyond that cluster, it's worth flagging as an outlier — and worth asking why. Sometimes an outlier is a measurement error; sometimes it's a completely real, interesting result.
Five values cluster tightly between 12 and 16, but the outlier at 40 stretches the range from 4 all the way to 28.
## Common Mistakes - Subtracting in the wrong order — range is always maximum minus minimum, so it's never negative. - Assuming any large or small-looking value is automatically an outlier without comparing it to where the rest of the data actually sits. - Removing outliers from a calculation without saying so — if you report a mean "without the outlier," always say that's what you did. ## Quick Gut-Check Range = max − min, and it only looks at the two extreme values. An outlier is a value far from the rest of the data, and it can inflate both the range and the mean far more than it inflates the median.

children.title: Choosing and Reading Graphs
children.summary: Circle graphs, bar graphs, line graphs, and scatter plots each answer a different kind of question about data. This lesson covers how to choose the right graph type for a data set and how to read specific values off each one.
children.content:
# Choosing and Reading Graphs ## The Idea Different graphs are built to answer different questions. Picking the right one — and knowing how to read values off it — is just as important as being able to draw it. Before choosing a graph, ask: what kind of question does this data answer? - **Circle graph (pie chart)** — best when your data represents **parts of a whole**, like how a monthly budget splits across categories. Each slice is a percent of the total, and all the slices add up to 100%. - **Bar graph** — best for **comparing separate categories**, like the number of students who prefer each of five sports. The height (or length) of each bar shows its value; categories don't have to be in any particular order. - **Line graph** — best for showing **change over time** (or another continuous variable), like a plant's height measured every week. The line connects points in order, so you can see whether values are rising, falling, or staying flat. - **Scatter plot** — best for showing a **relationship between two numeric variables**, like hours studied versus test score. Each point is one individual with two measurements; a pattern in the points (or lack of one) tells you whether the variables are related. ## Reading Values Off Each Graph - **Circle graph:** a slice's size is its percent of the whole — a slice labelled 25% is a quarter of the total, no matter what the total is. - **Bar graph:** trace the top of a bar straight across to the vertical axis to read its value. - **Line graph:** find the point above the time (or x-value) you care about, then trace across to the vertical axis. - **Scatter plot:** each dot is an (x, y) pair — trace down to the horizontal axis for one variable and across to the vertical axis for the other. ## Worked Example A survey asks 40 students their favourite way to get to school: ``` Walk: 16 students Bus: 12 students Bike: 8 students Car: 4 students ``` Since these are four separate categories that together make up "all 40 students," this data fits **either** a bar graph (easy to compare 16 vs. 12 vs. 8 vs. 4 directly) **or** a circle graph (to emphasize each group's share of the whole, e.g., Walk is 16/40 = 40% of students). If instead the question were "how did the number of students walking to school change from September to June," that's a value tracked **over time** — a line graph, not a bar or circle graph, is the right choice.
Four graph types, each built for a different kind of question: circle graphs for shares of a whole, bar graphs for comparing categories, line graphs for change over time, and scatter plots for relationships between two variables.
## Common Mistakes - Using a line graph for categories with no natural order (like favourite pizza toppings) — a line connecting unrelated categories is meaningless. - Using a circle graph when the values aren't parts of one single whole (e.g., totals from several different surveys). - Assuming a scatter plot always shows a straight-line pattern — sometimes the honest reading is "these two variables don't appear related at all." ## Quick Gut-Check Parts of a whole → circle graph. Comparing categories → bar graph. Change over time → line graph. Relationship between two variables → scatter plot.

children.title: Simple Interest
children.summary: Simple interest grows by a fixed amount every year, calculated with `I = Prt`. This lesson works through calculating interest and total value for both an investment and a loan, given a principal, an annual rate, and a number of years.
children.content:
# Simple Interest ## The Idea When you put money in a savings account, or borrow money from a bank, interest is the amount added on top — a percentage of the original amount, charged (or earned) for the time the money is invested or owed. **Simple interest** grows by the same fixed amount every year, calculated only on the original amount, called the **principal**. The formula: ``` I = P × r × t ``` where: - **I** is the interest earned (or owed), in dollars - **P** is the principal — the original amount invested or borrowed - **r** is the annual interest rate, written as a **decimal** (so 5% becomes 0.05) - **t** is the time, in years Once you know the interest, the **total value** — what the investment grows to, or what the loan grows to owe — is: ``` A = P + I ``` ## Worked Example Malia invests $800 in a savings account that pays 5% simple interest per year. How much is the account worth after 3 years? ``` P = 800 r = 5% = 0.05 t = 3 I = P × r × t I = 800 × 0.05 × 3 I = 40 × 3 I = 120 A = P + I A = 800 + 120 A = 920 ``` After 3 years, Malia has earned **$120** in interest, so her account is worth **$920**. Notice that the interest is the same, $40, every single year: $40 in year 1, $80 total by year 2, $120 total by year 3. That steady, unchanging yearly amount is what makes it "simple" interest — it never compounds on interest already earned, only on the original $800. ## A Second Example: Loans Work the Same Way Deion borrows $1200 at 4% simple interest for 2.5 years. How much will he owe in total when the loan is due? ``` I = 1200 × 0.04 × 2.5 = 120 A = 1200 + 120 = 1320 ``` Deion will owe **$1320** — the $1200 he borrowed plus $120 in interest.
An $800 principal earning 5% simple interest grows by the same $40 every year: $840, then $880, then $920.
## Common Mistakes - Forgetting to convert a percent to a decimal before multiplying (using 5 instead of 0.05 gives an answer 100 times too big). - Plugging in the total number of months instead of years for t — if a problem gives months, convert to years first (e.g., 18 months = 1.5 years). - Adding interest to the rate or principal incorrectly — always calculate I first, then add it to P to get A. A is never just P × r × t. ## Quick Gut-Check I = P × r × t gives you the interest earned or owed. A = P + I gives you the total amount after that interest is added. The rate must be a decimal, and the time must be in years.

children.title: Budgeting and Discounts
children.summary: Applying a percent discount and building a personal budget both come down to careful percent and subtraction work. This lesson walks through calculating a sale price after a discount and finding how much of a monthly income is left over as savings.
children.content:
# Budgeting and Discounts ## The Idea This lesson covers two everyday percent skills: figuring out a **discounted price**, and building a simple **personal budget**. **Discounts** reduce a price by a percentage. To find the discount amount, multiply the original price by the discount rate (as a decimal). To find the sale price, subtract that amount from the original price: ``` discount amount = original price × discount rate sale price = original price − discount amount ``` **Budgeting** compares income (money coming in) to expenses (money going out). Whatever is left over is what you save: ``` savings = income − expenses ``` A budget that balances doesn't mean spending everything you earn — a healthy budget usually leaves room for savings. ## Worked Example: Discount A jacket is priced at $80, and the store is running a 15% off sale. What's the sale price? ``` discount rate = 15% = 0.15 discount amount = 80 × 0.15 = 12 sale price = 80 − 12 = 68 ``` The jacket is on sale for **$68** — you save **$12** off the original price. A quick shortcut: since you're paying 100% − 15% = 85% of the original price, you can also compute the sale price directly as `80 × 0.85 = 68`. Both methods give the same answer — use whichever is easier to keep track of. ## Worked Example: Budget Priya works a part-time job and earns $650 in a month. Her monthly expenses are: ``` Phone plan: $40 Transit pass: $45 Food/snacks: $90 Clothes: $75 Entertainment: $60 Miscellaneous: $100 ``` Total expenses: ``` 40 + 45 + 90 + 75 + 60 + 100 = 410 ``` Amount saved: ``` savings = income − expenses savings = 650 − 410 savings = 240 ``` Priya saves **$240** that month. Tracking expenses this way, category by category, makes it easy to spot where a budget could be adjusted — for example, if Priya wanted to save more, cutting the miscellaneous category is an easy place to look first.
The $80 original price splits into the $68 you pay and the $12 discount removed — 15% of $80 is $12.
## Common Mistakes - Subtracting the discount **rate** from 100 correctly (100% − 15% = 85%) but then forgetting to convert it to a decimal (0.85) before multiplying. - Applying the discount percent to the sale price instead of the original price. - In a budget, forgetting to include small or irregular expenses — miscellaneous costs add up and change how much is actually left to save. ## Quick Gut-Check Discount amount = price × rate; sale price = price − discount amount (or price × (1 − rate) in one step). Savings = income − expenses.
